candidates.statement: Establishments should consider the severity of each observation and prioritize corrective actions 195 accordingly, which might include grouping issues or taking a systemic approach to corrective 196 actions. Some observations may be clustered, such as in general categories (e.g., investigations, 197 cleanrooms, staff competencies) or systems (quality, production, facilities and equipment, 198 packaging and labeling, materials, and laboratory control). Establishments should also examine 199 past inspections and internal audits for repeat observations or similar observation trends. 200 Identifying categories and trends may highlight a systemic issue at a facility or within an 201 organization. There are quality risk management 19 tools which may be useful to assist in 202 clustering and prioritizing observations (e.g., cause-and-effect analysis). 203
candidates.context: IV. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ADDRESSING FDA 483 OBSERVATIONS 193 Establishments should determine if deficiencies described in an observation affect other drugs, 205 processes, or associated facilities and contract organizations and expand their investigations 206 accordingly. As investigations proceed, additional gathered or obtained information may 207 indicate that changes should be made to the initial risk assessment and the investigation plan. 208 (see section IV.C, Develop an Investigation Plan and Conduct an Investigation). 209

During and immediately after the close of an inspection, an establishment’s 232 management should fully understand all observations and assess any related risks to product 233 quality and patient safety. Establishments should take timely and appropriate actions based on 234 this risk assessment. Actions may include, but are not limited to, notifying customers, recalling 235 drugs, conducting additional testing, adding lots to stability programs, design improvements 236 (e.g., process, equipment, or facility), amending or supplementing drug application or master 237 files, enhanced complaint monitoring, and labeling revisions. If applicable, establishments that 238 manufacture animal drugs should perform a risk assessment of the animals receiving the drug as 239 well as any person handling the drug or humans consuming the products of food-producing 240 animals. 22

candidates.statement: FDA recommends establishments prepare an investigation plan and include a detailed protocol 289 and methodology. A comprehensive investigation using the prepared investigation plan 290 demonstrates to FDA that an establishment is addressing the observations and the underlying 291 issue(s). This plan should include a scientifically justified and risk-based scope, including 292 justification for any part of an establishment’s operations that is excluded from the investigation. 293
candidates.context: C. Develop an Investigation Plan and Conduct an Investigation 287 For finished drugs, 21 CFR 211.192 requires a thorough investigation of issues such as an 295 unexplained discrepancy or the failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its 296 specifications (and investigation of other batches of the same drug product and other drug 297 products that may have been associated with the specific failure or discrepancy). A written 298 record of the investigation is also required, including its conclusions and follow-up. 25 Toward 299 this end, a comprehensive investigation plan addressing FDA 483 observations also generally 300 includes identifying any related trends, linking any connected FDA 483 observations, assessing 301

candidates.statement: risks, and analyzing root causes. 26 , 27 FDA recommends that the same approach should be used 302 for other drugs. 28
candidates.context: A risk assessment helps establishments identify and understand the potential effect an 305 observation has on patient safety, manufactured drugs (whether or not they have been 306 distributed), and future drug quality. 29

candidates.statement: Preventing recurrence of an observation is based on determining the root cause(s); addressing the 316 most obvious causal factor is often not sufficient. A methodical approach to identifying the root 317 cause(s) is important, including identifying potential causes (there may be more than one), 318 investigating each potential cause individually, and testing product or systems using 319 scientifically supported approaches for verification. An establishment should be aware of and 320 minimize bias in risk evaluation and decision-making when determining root cause. For 321 example, testing that only supports the first hypothesized root cause may exclude the real (or 322 complete) root cause and may bias the interpretation of data. The real (or complete) root cause 323 may not be investigated, which could lead to additional CGMP failures. 30
candidates.context: For example, an inspectional observation cited that a particular piece of equipment was cleaned 309 improperly.
